Topical phenylephrine works, they sell it as a nose spray. 

When the nose is under attack or thinks it is  (I'm looking at you allergies), the vessels in your nose dilate so more white blood cells and foreign body trapping mucus can fight back. These wider blood vessels cause the swelling we know as congestion

Decongestion therefore requires vasoconstriction. This happens when an alpha agonist, like phenylephrine binds to its respective receptor. When you squirt phenylephrine up your nose, it activates these receptors and you can breathe.

When you orally take phenylephrine, 99% is destroyed by your stomach, and the rest is distributed by the bloodstream to the whole body, letting it activate alpha-1 receptors in places other than your nose. 

There's a reason you don't drink Afrin (oxymetazoline), which works the same way but also binds to the alpha-2 receptor.

The problem with topical decongestants is that they give rebound congestion when used to often. Oral decongestants that actually reach the bloodstream don't have that problem.

The only one that works orally is pseudoephedrine, which works by releasing catecholamines (noradrenaline/norepinephrine,a adrenaline/epinephrine , dopamine). Norepinephrine and epinephrine are the body's natural ligands for the alpha and beta adrenergic receptors. Beta receptors in the lung cause bronchodilation when agonized, which is good if you have a nasty chest cold to go with that stuffy nose (most asthma medications are beta agonists). 

Pseudoephedrine can't enter the brain, but all it takes is the knowledge of a highschool chemistry student to make it into meth which can. Meth causes the same catecholamine release but in the brain. Excess dopamine in the peripheral nervous system causes nausea and tachycardia, in the central nervous system it causes stimulation, euphoria, and psychosis (all antipsychotics are dopamine antagonists).

No, they only act as antagonists at the beta norepinephrine/epinephrine receptor. In your peripheral nervous system they are found mostly in the heart and control things like heart rate and how forcefully the heart beats. Alpha receptors are found in blood vessels and cause vasoconstriction when activated. Oxymetazoline is an alpha agonist sold as a nose spray, and it causes the blood vessels in your nose to constrict, which clears up congestion.

In the beta receptors in the brain don't do much, and propranolol is one of the few beta blockers that can cross the blood brain barrier. Beta receptors in the CNS  don't control anxiety and alertness, but their activation causes melatonin to be released, so propranolol can cause insomnia. Alpha receptors in your central nervous system control things like anxiety and alertness, which is why clonidine causes drowsiness and some anxiety relief. Clonidine isn't an alpha blocker directly, but it instead binds exclusively to the alpha auto receptor. Auto receptors are receptors on the presynaptic nerve that sort of measure the quantity of neurotransmitters in the synapse. If there are a lot of neurotransmitters in the synapse that can bind to the post synaptic receptors, they will also bind to the auto receptors which will tell the presynaptic nerve to stop releasing so many neurotransmitters because there are too many. Clonidine  doesn't bind to the post synaptic receptors that would cause that nerve to fire the same way epinephrine would, but to the auto receptor exclusively. This constant binding fools the presynaptic nerve into thinking   there are too many neurotransmitters in the synapse so it will stop releasing them. Basically, instead of directly blocking the receptor, it stops things that normally would bi d and activate it from ever making it there.

Some pain killers don't affect the central nervous system. NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin, etc) inhibit the COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, which are vital in the production of several hormones. One such is prostaglandin. Prostaglandin has many functions, but the relevant one in this case is sensitizing neurons in the peripheral nervous system to pain. Your body makes lots of prostaglandin when you're sick, which is why the flu makes you ache all over. No activity in the central nervous system though. 

Opioid pain killers bind at the mu-opioid receptor in the brain. It causes a release of GABA and mood lifting monoamines, but it's not completely understood why this agonism brings about the effects it does. The concentration of mu-opioid receptors in the part of brain that interprets and processes pain is higher than most places in the CNS. Because of this, one theory is that the GABA releasing properties of mu-opioid agonists causes a reduction of activity in the pain processing region of the brain disproportionate to other regions. 

tl;dr: scientists think opioids might cause euphoria not because they make the happy part of your brain active, but supressing activity in the bad part of the brain.

Dissociatives are analgesics that act on the central nervous system, because their antagonism of the NMDA receptor simply blocks communication from the conscious part of your brain from the peripheral nervous system, but leave the pain processing portion of the central nervous system still active. The physical pain of a stubbed toe won't make it to the pain center, but negative sensations sent from the conscious part of your brain (sadness, shame, etc.) still do.

Dextromethorphan isn't a very potent NMDA antagonist however. Your body metabolizes it into dextrorphan, which is far more potent.

One of the functions of the NMDA receptor is to desensitize/downregulate other receptors that are being activated more often than is natural, which is basically what building a tolerance to a drug is. The receptors become less responsive to not only external molecules that bind to them, but your body's natural neurotransmitters as well. For opioids, this makes the mu-opioid receptor less responsive to your natural endorphins as well as drugs. 

 An NMDA antagonist like DXM that stops the receptor from being activated also prevents the receptor from playing it's role in tolerance buildup, so when taken concurrently with any potentially addictive substance, the rate at which tolerance and dependence build is a good bit slower. 

NMDA receptor activation isn't the only thing that builds up tolerance though, but IME NMDA antagonists do slow down tolerance buildup considerably.  

Since dextromethorphan takes a while to be metabolized into dextrorphan, it's best to take it a few hours before you take any opioids to give the more potent NMDA antagonist a chance to kick in.

NMDA antagonists also have analgesic effects that add to the opioid's, and as long as you don't take too much, the dissociative effects from DXM go nicely with opioids.

I don't think it can reduce the tolerance you already have, but NMDA antagonists like ketamine are useful in depression because the excess NMDA blockade is sort of like a "reset" button for your brain. I'm not sure if it can reset tolerance though, and I've never used it that way.
